issues.item: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma profile, 'Medical Procedures' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report. The memory items describe classic reliving/terror reactions, and the formulation shows a strong Memory → Triggers link, implying triggers should plausibly cue the stalking memory. 'Loud noises' and possibly 'happy families' can occur idiosyncratically, but a medical examination trigger is clinically disconnected from stalking unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere. This makes the trigger set less coherent with the trauma type and formulation.

vignette:
Mai first met him at a networking event after the markets closed. He was a consultant who worked with a firm that occasionally crossed her desk, and for a few weeks she considered him charming. She agreed to dinner twice, then declined a third invitation, and that was when something shifted. He began appearing outside her office building. Then at the coffee cart she visited every morning. Then he started sending emails to her work account, long ones, describing in detail what he imagined she was doing at home with her partner. The night he broke into her apartment, she had just gotten out of the shower. She heard the back door splinter — a crack so sharp it seemed to split the air itself — and then she smelled him before she saw him, the sour alcohol on his breath as he stood in her hallway, holding a kitchen knife he had taken from her own block. Her partner was away on a business trip. She managed to lock herself in the bathroom and call the police, but the minutes she spent pressed against the door, listening to him talk through the wood in that low, calm voice, carved something into her that she has not been able to smooth over since.

He was arrested, convicted, and is still incarcerated. That should have ended it. But Mai has come to feel that the real haunting began after he was gone. The memory of that night does not stay in the past. When it surfaces — and it surfaces without warning, triggered by a car backfiring on the street or a glass bottle dropped in a restaurant — she is back in the bathroom, the terror flooding her body exactly as it did then, her heart slamming, her hands numb, the smell of alcohol suddenly thick in her nostrils even when no one nearby has been drinking. She knows, intellectually, that it is 2025 and she is safe in her own living room. But knowing that does not stop the memory from overriding everything. The experience feels so extreme, so vivid, that part of her still struggles to believe it truly happened to her. It has the quality of a nightmare, not a real event, yet her body reacts as though it is happening right now.

Her work as a stock broker has become increasingly difficult. The trading floor at her firm is filled with loud, sudden noises — shouts, phones slamming, alarms — and every unexpected sound sends her into a state of hypervigilance that makes it impossible to focus on the numbers on her screen. She has started arriving early and leaving before the closing bell so she can avoid the worst of it. Her supervisor has noticed the drop in her trade volume and has asked if something is wrong. Mai has not told him. She is not sure she could explain it without sounding unhinged.

Socially, she has withdrawn. She used to enjoy weekend brunches with her partner, but now she scans every restaurant for the smell of alcohol before she can sit down, and if she catches even a whiff of beer or whiskey, she has to leave immediately. Her partner has been patient, but she has seen the disappointment in his eyes when she cancels yet another dinner. What frightens her most, though, is the way she has come to feel about happy families. Seeing a couple with children in a park, or a family laughing together at a café, now fills her with a dread she cannot name and a sense of exclusion that feels like grief. She had wanted children herself, someday. Now she is terrified that the version of herself that could trust the world enough to bring a child into it does not exist anymore.

It was her partner who finally convinced her to call a therapist. She came to the first session with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her posture careful. She said she wanted to stop feeling like the woman in the bathroom. She was not sure if that was possible, but she was willing to try.
